extracted.intended_audience: Members of Congress, congressional staff, and policymakers evaluating A-76 competitive sourcing policy and legislation
extracted.subtask_description: Policy guidance and recommended legislative/administrative options for Congress and executive agencies on conducting, reporting, and reforming OMB Circular A-76 public-private competitions, with special attention to military medical facilities, cost comparison rules, employee rights, and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require specific reporting on the status of ongoing A-76 competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may direct DOD to provide more detailed information on the status of ongoing A-76 studies, including quarterly updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requested reporting items include: the number of older competitions under review and whether these competitions have been granted waivers; the status of new standard multi-function A-76 studies, including how many competitions are in excess of the 12-month limitation and how many have been granted waivers; the number of competitions that are in excess of 18 months, with or without waivers; the number of competitions in excess of 30-months, with or without waivers; and the demographics of the affected government employees in A-76 competitions and whether any particular group of employees are adversely impacted by the A-76 policy, competition process or the final outcome. (References: Section proposing quarterly update; Section 327 of H.R. 1585 broadening DOD annual report.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit establishment of numerical quotas for A-76 studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could prohibit the establishment of numerical quotas for federal agencies that drive the conduct of A-76 competitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Some argue that pressure to meet PMA or OMB-imposed numerical targets may influence agencies to continue or initiate competitions despite other priorities or problems. Legislative option: Section 328 of H.R. 1585 would prohibit OMB-imposed quotas on DOD A-76 competitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine activities at military medical facilities to be inherently governmental
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could determine that any activities on military medical facilities that affect patient care would be considered inherently governmental and not appropriate for competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include declaring all activities at military medical facilities 'inherently governmental' and not subject to competition, or imposing a one-year moratorium on future A-76 competitions at military medical facilities (example: Rep. Solomon Ortiz amendment in H.R. 1538). Rationale: activities touching the military patient (e.g., maintenance that affects morale or care) may be too critical to outsource.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit inclusion of health care and retirement costs in A-76 cost comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could prohibit the inclusion of health care and retirement costs in the cost comparison process used for A-76 competitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reportedly the Army failed to exclude health care costs where required by Defense Appropriations language. Legislative option: Section 324 of H.R. 1585 would exclude health care and retirement costs in the cost comparison process (though it would not require contractors to provide the same level of benefits as DOD). The exclusion aims to avoid rewarding contractors providing lesser benefits and to comply with appropriations direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a team of acquisition professionals to serve as Agency Tender Officials (ATOs)
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB could establish a team of experienced A-76 professionals who could be called upon to serve as ATOs, potentially serving outside their assigned federal agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATOs should be selected to serve in competitions outside their home agency, require sufficient funds to represent federal employees throughout the competition (including post-award), and have a certain degree of independence. This addresses the observation that no single individual had overall authority in complex competitions (e.g., Walter Reed) and that local officials lacked expertise and resources to pursue appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require enforcement of A-76 rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could ensure that the rules governing the conduct of A-76 studies are followed and that there is authority to enforce them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rules are not followed there is no authority to ensure compliance, undermining process integrity. Examples: OMB or DoD might have stopped Walter Reed competition when it exceeded permitted length; the Army could have excluded health care costs as required by law. Enforcement mechanisms and clear authority are recommended so the process and outcomes retain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant federal employees the same protest/appeal rights as private sector contractors
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could grant federal employees direct protest and appeal rights (similar to contractors) to challenge privatization decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the time of the Walter Reed competition, contractors could protest to GAO while federal employees could not directly protest; ATOs were intended to represent employees but lacked standing in some cases. Legislative option: Section 329 of H.R. 1585 would give federal employees some appeal rights to have privatization decisions reviewed by GAO; a majority of employees could choose a representative to appeal decisions to GAO and intervene before the Court of Federal Claims. Also consider prohibiting agencies from conducting competitions unless they have sufficient funds to fund representation for federal employees throughout all phases, including post-award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage alternatives to A-76 (e.g., high-performing organizations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could provide encouragement and incentives for agencies to explore appropriate alternatives to A-76 competitions, such as creating High-Performing Organizations (HPOs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GAO’s Commercial Activities Panel recommended development of HPOs. Given that federal employees are now winning the majority of competitions, agencies might pursue alternatives that avoid costs and challenges of A-76 while achieving efficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancel outstanding A-76 studies conducted under the pre-2003 Circular
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could direct the cancellation of any outstanding competitions conducted under the pre-2003 A-76 Circular to avoid protracted or flawed reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Competitions under the pre-2003 rules have sometimes taken excessive time (example: an eight-year review at Keesler AFB). The recommendation is to cancel such pending studies to prevent further harm and process compromise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow DoD to opt out of A-76 during declared war or military mobilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The A-76 Circular provides that the Department of Defense Competitive Sourcing Official shall determine if the circular applies to DoD during times of declared war or military mobilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Had DoD exercised this option to exclude itself, significant personnel shortages at Walter Reed and similar effects might have been avoided. Policy criterion: enable suspension/exclusion of A-76 application to DoD when wartime operational demands warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply minimum cost differential and account for transition/disruption costs in cost comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost comparisons should account for minimum cost differentials and other costs associated with disruption and loss of productivity due to competition processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observers (e.g., AFGE lobbyist John Threlkeld) stated the Army’s analysis failed to account for the $10 million 'minimum cost differential' federal rules require to be applied to contractor bids to account for disruption and productivity loss. The report also documents transition and compensation costs (e.g., MEDCOM costs, VERA/VSIP, severance pay) and notes that such extraordinary expenses should be considered when evaluating net savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that A-76 is not appropriate for all activities; evaluate mission-critical risk
rubrics_metrics.description: If A-76 policy is to work effectively it cannot be used for every federal activity; competitions may be inappropriate for mission-critical activities (particularly those affecting military health care).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: consider exempting base operations support and functions that touch military patients (maintenance, repair, trash removal in medical settings) from competitions because the risks of mission failure and impacts on morale/patient care are high. Policy decisions should weigh mission criticality and operational risk, not only cost savings.
